source_metadata.title: Treatment of Children with Primary Immunodeficiencies with a Subcutaneous Immunoglobulin 16.5% (Cutaquig® [Octanorm])
source_metadata.source_type: pediatric subanalysis of a prospective, open-label, single-arm Phase III clinical study

atoms.canonical_statement: The pediatric subanalysis evaluated whether once-weekly cutaquig prevented serious bacterial infections in children with primary antibody deficiencies and also characterized cutaquig pharmacokinetics.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The main objective was to assess the efficacy of cutaquig in preventing serious bacterial infections.

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary objectives included safety and tolerability, nonserious infection frequency, and health-related quality of life.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Secondary objectives included evaluation of safety and tolerability, the number and rate of other nonserious infections

atoms.canonical_statement: Pediatric participants were enrolled within a prospective, open-label, single-arm Phase III study conducted at 20 centers in Europe and North America.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: prospective, open-label, single-arm, Phase III study (NCT01888484) at 20 centers in Europe and North America

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligible pediatric patients had primary antibody deficiencies, were stable on IVIG for at least six infusions, and had IgG trough concentrations of at least 5.0 g/L before switching to cutaquig.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: patients with PADs, stable on IVIG treatment for at least six infusions (with IgG trough levels ≥5.0 g/l)

population.label: Pediatric patients with primary antibody deficiencies stable on IVIG
inclusion_criteria: Stable IVIG treatment for at least six infusions

atoms.canonical_statement: The treatment schedule consisted of a 12-week wash-in/wash-out period followed by a 52-week efficacy period.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: underwent a 12-week wash-in/-out period, followed by a 52-week efficacy period

atoms.canonical_statement: During both study periods, cutaquig was administered once weekly at 1.5 times the previous monthly IVIG dose divided into four equal weekly subcutaneous infusions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: received cutaquig doses at 1.5-times their previous monthly IVIG dose divided into four equal weekly SCIG infusions

exposures.details: 1.5 times previous monthly IVIG dose divided into four equal weekly doses

atoms.canonical_statement: Serious bacterial infection was defined as bacterial pneumonia, bacteremia/sepsis, osteomyelitis/septic arthritis, visceral abscess, or bacterial meningitis.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: SBIs were defined as bacterial pneumonia, bacteremia/sepsis, osteomyelitis/septic arthritis, visceral abscess and bacterial meningitis

outcome.definition: Bacterial pneumonia, bacteremia/sepsis, osteomyelitis/septic arthritis, visceral abscess, or bacterial meningitis

atoms.canonical_statement: All analyses were descriptive; missing data were not imputed, and person-year calculations used collected values only.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: All data were analyzed descriptively. Missing data were not imputed and calculations pertaining to person-year computations were based on collected values only.

atoms.canonical_statement: Infection-rate analyses excluded infections occurring during the 12-week wash-in/wash-out period so that efficacy-period infections reflected steady-state cutaquig treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Infection rate calculations were limited to the efficacy period

atoms.canonical_statement: The analysis included 38 pediatric patients: 12 aged 2 to <6 years, 14 aged 6 to <12 years, and 12 aged 12 to <17 years.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The current analysis included 38 pediatric patients

atoms.canonical_statement: Thirty-four of 38 patients completed the study; four adolescents withdrew, three for personal reasons and one for noncompliance.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Thirty four patients completed the study. Four adolescent patients withdrew from the study

atoms.canonical_statement: Across all 38 patients, mean age was 8.7 ± 4.2 years (range 2.0-16.0) and mean body weight was 36.4 ± 18.9 kg (range 13.0-86.4).
The cohort was 23.7% female and 76.3% male.
Primary immunodeficiency diagnoses were common variable immunodeficiency in 20 patients (52.6%), X-linked agammaglobulinemia in 6 (15.8%), and other diagnoses in 12 (31.6%).
Twenty-three patients (60.5%) were enrolled in Europe and 15 (39.5%) in North America.
Before study SCIG, 33 patients (86.8%) had received IVIG every 4 weeks, four (10.5%) every 3 weeks, and the mean dose over the last six IVIG infusions was 424 mg/kg every 3 or 4 weeks.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The mean dose of IVIG during the last six infusions prior to switching to SCIG was 424 mg/kg every 3 or 4 weeks.

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the study, 38 patients received 2213 cutaquig infusions; the median number per patient was 64 (mean 58, range 3-65), at a mean dose of 161 ± 54 mg/kg per infusion (range 60-290).

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The total number of infusions of cutaquig was 2213.

atoms.canonical_statement: For all patients, mean active infusion duration was 84.2 ± 45.9 minutes, mean maximum volume was 38.4 ± 20.2 mL, mean maximum volume per site was 15.4 ± 5.2 mL/site, and mean maximum infusion flow rate was 39.4 ± 11.1 mL/h.
Dosing compliance was high: 26 patients (68.4%) received at least 64 scheduled infusions and eight (21.1%) received 61-63 infusions; the four early terminators received fewer infusions.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Compliance with the prescribed dosing schedule was high.

atoms.canonical_statement: One needle was used for 8.6% of infusions and two needles for 61.3%; among children aged 2 to <6 years, one or two sites were used for 99.2% of administrations.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The majority of infusions were administered using one or two needles

atoms.canonical_statement: Across 2213 infusions, the left abdomen was used in 64.5%, right abdomen in 60.5%, left thigh in 21.0%, and right thigh in 21.3%; more than one site could be used per infusion.

exposures.details: Multiple administration sites permitted per infusion

atoms.canonical_statement: No serious bacterial infections occurred during either the 52-week efficacy period or the wash-in/wash-out period, representing 35 person-years of exposure.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: No SBIs occurred in any patients during the efficacy period or during the wash-in/-out period (35 person-years of exposure).

quantitative_result.original_result_text: No SBIs occurred in any patients during the efficacy period or during the wash-in/-out period.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors interpreted the observed infection rate as approximating the general pediatric population and concluded that the study objective of preventing serious and severe bacterial infections was met.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This suggests that IgG supplementation with cutaquig was effective in ‘normalizing’ the rate of infections

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors reported mean IgG trough concentrations of approximately 11-13 g/L during once-weekly cutaquig and considered the approximately 161 mg/kg weekly regimen sufficient to maintain trough concentrations above 5-6 g/L.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: mean IgG trough levels were 11–13 g/l for children treated with once-weekly infusions of cutaquig

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors emphasized individualized dose adjustment to body weight in children because infusion duration, volume, and flow rate increased with age and weight.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: This highlights the importance of individualizing SCIG therapy and continuously adjusting the dose to weight, especially in children.

atoms.canonical_statement: Concomitant antibiotic therapy was allowed and may have affected the observed infection frequency.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: patients were allowed to receive concomitant treatment with antibiotics, which may have affected the observed infection frequency.

atoms.canonical_statement: Because data were collected across multiple sites, differences in clinical practice between sites and geographical regions may have affected study outcomes.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: differences in clinical practice between sites and geographical regions may have affected the outcomes of our study.

atoms.canonical_statement: The relatively small pediatric sample limited statistical power and may have led to underestimation of rare adverse events.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The relatively small sample size limits the statistical power of our analysis and may lead to the underestimation of rare AEs.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that once-weekly 16.5% SCIG cutaquig was safe, efficacious, and tolerable in pediatric patients with primary antibody deficiencies.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: these results demonstrate the safety, efficacy and tolerability of once-weekly infusions of 16.5% SCIG cutaquig in pediatric patients with PADs.
